50-032.r: Parathyroid glands work independently of the pituitary; parathyroid hormone (with calcitonin from thyroid) regulates calcium in blood and bones.

50-033.r: Iodised salt (table salt + a little iodine salt) is useful because it controls the thyroid gland; iodine deficiency causes thyroid problems.

50-034.r: Goitre (enlarged thyroid) is endemic in hilly areas because their soil, water and crops are iodine-deficient → A and R true, R explains A.

50-035.r: Thyroxine → main hormone of the thyroid gland; controls metabolism, heart, brain development; its deficiency causes cretinism and myxedema.

50-036.r: Iodine-containing hormones → thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), made by the thyroid from iodine + the amino acid tyrosine (so thyroxine is an amino acid derivative).

50-039.r: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid to secrete thyroxine.

50-040.r: Adrenaline → anger, fear, danger; estrogen → females; insulin → glucose; pheromones → attracting partners through sense of smell.

50-041.r: Adrenaline (epinephrine) from adrenal glands → 'fight or flight' hormone; raises heartbeat, causes excitement, dilates vessels to brain, muscles, heart.

50-043.r: Estrogen (a hormone) → released mainly by ovarian follicles; also by corpus luteum and placenta; develops female secondary sexual characteristics.

50-045.r: Female sex hormone → estrogen (oestrogen), made mainly by the ovaries; develops female reproductive organs and sexual characteristics.

50-046.r: Estrone → a weak (postmenopausal) estrogen, so a female sex hormone; testosterone (androgen) is male; thyroxine regulates metabolism.

50-047.r: After menopause ovaries stop estrogen and progesterone but still make a little testosterone; adrenal androstenedione becomes estrone. The book gives no single answer (*).

50-048.r: True: somatotropin (growth hormone) rises with exercise; men's testes make some progesterone; women's adrenals secrete testosterone. Statement 4 (stress lowers cortisol) is false.

50-049.r: Hormone → testosterone; enzyme → lipase; phospholipid → lecithin; polymer → polythene.

50-050.r: Parathyroid hormone (PTH; 84 amino acids, from chief cells) regulates blood calcium and phosphate; makes kidneys excrete more phosphate.

50-051.r: Melatonin (pineal gland) rises in darkness and drops in bright light; bright light during sleep is undesirable → A true, R false.

50-052.r: Pheromones → chemicals released by animals, especially insects, that affect the behaviour of others of the same species.

51-001.r: Fertilization occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube), at its end near the ovary, away from the uterus.

51-002.r: Sperm normally fertilizes the ovum in the fallopian tube (oviduct or uterine tube), not in the cervix or uterus; the tube carries the egg from the ovary.

51-003.r: Sperm stays alive up to about 72 hours in the female tract but can fertilize for about 48 hours (one to two days).

51-004.r: Embryo's heart starts beating about 4-5 weeks after fertilization (fourth week), at about 105-121 beats per minute.

51-005.r: Amnion → membrane filled with amniotic fluid (amniotic sac); protects the embryo from desiccation and outer pressure.

51-006.r: Sertoli cells → 'nurse' cells of the testis (in seminiferous tubules); support spermatogenesis; activated by FSH.

52-001.r: Chlorophyll contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and magnesium – not calcium.

52-002.r: Chlorophyll contains magnesium (needed to make it); magnesium deficiency → yellowing of leaves between the veins.

52-004.r: Chloroplasts can self-replicate because they contain both DNA and RNA.

52-005.r: Chlorophyll's job in photosynthesis → absorbing light (usually sunlight); it sits in the chloroplasts.

52-006.r: Dark reaction (light-independent; Calvin cycle or Blackman's reaction) → stroma of the chloroplast; light reactions → thylakoids.

52-007.r: Photosynthesis: main product glucose; by-product oxygen (O2); occurs in chloroplasts.

52-008.r: Photosynthesis turns light energy into chemical energy stored in food; the glucose made soon turns into starch or sucrose → A and R true, R explains A.

52-009.r: Oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water (splitting of water molecules), not from CO2.

52-010.r: Photosynthesis → plants take in CO2 and release O2 while forming glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆); light energy is stored in the bonds of sugar.

52-016.r: Radiant energy absorbed by plants → photolysis of water: H2O molecules split into hydrogen ions and oxygen gas.

52-017.r: Most of Earth's oxygen → algae: about 90% of photosynthesis is by aquatic plants and algae (85% in sea, 5% in rivers, ponds).

52-018.r: Only II true: marine phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria make about 50% of world's oxygen; oceans, not rainforests, produce more; III is false.

52-019.r: Photosynthesis can occur day or night – it needs light: sunlight, moonlight (marine algae) or even electric light; it is how plants make food.

52-022.r: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts (which hold chlorophyll), mainly in leaves (broad lamina), partly in stems.

52-023.r: Plants strongly absorb blue and red light (also violet); photosynthesis is least or nil in green light.

52-024.r: Chlorophyll absorbs red (long wavelength) and blue (short wavelength) light; green is reflected, so plants look green.

52-025.r: Most effective light for photosynthesis → red, then blue; nil in green; T.W. Engelmann (1888) showed the action spectrum using algae.
52-025.t: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red, but the single most active light is red, not blue or violet.

52-028.r: Artificial (electric) light can bring about photosynthesis; marine algae can even use moonlight.

52-029.r: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy: CO2 + H2O → glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) + O2.

52-030.r: Making one glucose molecule in photosynthesis uses 18 ATP, 6 CO2 and 12 NADPH.
52-030.h: Steps of six: CO2 6, NADPH 12, ATP 18.

52-031.r: Chloroplast converts solar energy into ATP: light reactions of photosynthesis turn light into chemical energy as ATP and NADPH.

52-034.r: Photosynthesis converts solar (light) energy into chemical energy – a form of potential energy stored in chemical bonds.

52-035.r: Photosynthesis → free energy of sunlight converted into potential (chemical) energy and stored; ultimate source of metabolic energy for all life.

52-036.r: Chlorella (single-celled green alga, class Chlorophyceae) → maximum efficiency in converting solar to chemical energy among the options.

52-037.r: Roots do not photosynthesise (no chloroplasts); they absorb water and nutrients; photosynthesis happens in leaves.

52-038.r: Photosynthesis removes CO2; respiration, decay of organic matter and volcanic action (outgassing) add CO2 to the carbon cycle.

52-039.r: Don't sleep under trees at night: no photosynthesis at night, but trees keep respiring and release CO2, so oxygen nearby falls.

52-041.r: Some bacteria (e.g. deep-sea green sulphur bacteria) use invisible infrared radiation for photosynthesis.

53-001.r: Wrong pair: 'thick, hard stem branching near base' = shrub, not tree (tree branches high up). Petiole attaches leaf to stem; creeper has a weak stem.

53-002.r: Stem transports food, stores food made by leaves, gives shape and support, bears leaves, flowers, fruits → 'more than one of the above'.

53-003.r: Plants absorb most water through root hairs, the outermost layer of the zone of cell maturation.

53-004.r: All three true: stomata = small pores in leaf epidermis, each ringed by two guard cells; gas exchange and transpiration happen through stomata.

53-005.r: Stomata open or close due to change in the amount of water in guard cells (turgor pressure from osmosis); swollen, turgid guard cells open them.

53-006.r: Water rises to great heights in trees by the suction pull of transpiration (loss of water vapour through stomata).

53-007.r: Ring-removing the bark cuts the phloem (food-carrying tissue in the bark) → food cannot reach roots, roots starve of energy, tree dies.

53-008.r: Water is conducted in vascular plants by xylem, which carries water and minerals from roots and replaces water lost in transpiration.

53-009.r: Xylem → carries water and dissolved minerals from roots to stem, leaves and other parts; transport is one-way (upward).

53-010.r: Xylem transports water (and minerals) from the soil to stems and leaves, and gives mechanical support; phloem is the other transport tissue.

53-012.r: Phloem ('bast') → carries food made in leaves to all parts; made of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres, phloem parenchyma.

53-013.r: Phloem → living tissue that carries organic food from leaves to the rest of the plant; xylem is made of dead cells.

53-014.r: A nail in a tree trunk stays at the same height: trees lengthen only at tips (apical meristems); the trunk only widens (lateral meristems).

53-015.r: Plants get nutrients mainly from soil; of seventeen essential elements, carbon, oxygen, hydrogen come from air, the rest (e.g. nitrogen) from soil.

53-016.r: Sodium is not essential for plants. Macronutrients: C, H, O, N, P, K, Mg, Ca, S – so potassium is a macronutrient and magnesium is not a micronutrient.

53-020.r: Sulphur → most useful nutrient for raising oil content in mustard (role in oil synthesis in seeds).

53-021.r: Plants take nitrogen mainly as nitrate (NO3–) ions from soil; atmospheric nitrogen gas is not directly available to most plants.

53-024.r: Phosphorus → stimulates early growth: promotes root development and hastens maturity; nitrogen → rapid leaf and stem growth.

53-025.r: Boron (micronutrient) → needed for nodule formation in legumes, new cell growth in meristems and sugar translocation.

53-026.r: Cuscuta (dodder) → parasitic plant: thin, leafless-looking yellow stems, leaves reduced to minute scales; feeds through haustoria.

53-027.r: Cuscuta (Amarbel) = rootless parasitic angiosperm; its haustoria tap host's xylem and phloem for food, water, minerals – not leaves → A true, R false.

53-028.r: Crop logging → plant analysis to assess nutrient needs for crop production; developed by Clements (USA) for sugarcane in Hawaii.

54-001.r: Insulin (from pancreas, regulates blood glucose) is not a plant hormone; cytokinin, ethylene and gibberellin are plant hormones.

54-002.r: Plant hormones: auxins, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid, ethylene; insulin, thyroxine, estrogen are not plant hormones.

54-005.r: Auxin → apical dominance; gibberellin → cell elongation; cytokinin → cell division; abscisic acid → growth inhibition.
54-005.h: Cytokinin sounds like cytokinesis = cell division.

54-006.r: Abscisic acid → drought tolerance ('stress hormone'); closes stomata when water is short (antitranspirant); discovered in the early 1960s.

54-007.r: Ethylene → plant hormone (phytohormone) found in gaseous form.

54-008.r: Artificial ripening gas (book's answer) → acetylene, from calcium carbide; banned under food adulteration rules, 1955. Natural ripening hormone → ethylene.

54-011.r: Ethrel (ethephon) → releases ethylene gas inside the plant; used to ripen bananas, mangoes, tomatoes quickly and uniformly.
54-011.t: IBA is a rooting hormone and maleic hydrazide prevents sprouting; neither ripens fruit.

54-012.r: Seedless tomatoes → spraying hormones (gibberellin, auxin or cytokinin) on flowers = artificial parthenocarpy.

55-001.r: Best plant part to study meiosis → anthers (pollen, the immature male gametophyte, forms after meiosis).

55-002.r: Vegetative propagation gives a clonal population and can be done most of the year (1, 3 true); it does not eliminate viruses – it spreads them.

55-003.r: Gootee = air layering (marcotting) → vegetative propagation by rooting an aerial stem while it is still attached to the parent plant.

55-004.r: Sugarcane: 'bud chip settlings' raised in a nursery save much seed material; settlings can also come from tissue culture (1 and 4 correct).

55-005.r: Sugarcane → short day plant (blooms in winter); more exactly an intermediate daylength plant with quantitative short-day behaviour.

55-006.r: Crop rotation: a legume must be followed by a non-legume (2 true); a deep-rooted crop should not be followed by the same type (1 false).

55-007.r: Pulses (deep tap roots, slow early growth) act as complementary crops when intercropped with cereals; A and R true, R not the correct explanation.

55-008.r: Clonal selection → used for asexually propagated crops like potato (selected plants give new clones).

55-009.r: Plant bud → an undeveloped (embryonic) shoot, found in a leaf axil or at the stem tip.

55-010.r: Embryo is found in seeds; after germination it grows into a new plant.

55-011.r: Fruit → ovary; seed → ovule; wood → stem; starch → leaf.
55-011.h: Bigger from bigger: ovary → fruit; smaller ovule → seed.

55-012.r: Stem cutting (vegetative propagation) gives plants identical to the parent – only one parent; seeds come from sexual propagation.

55-013.r: Sugarcane → grown by stem cuttings; mango and cotton from seeds; banana from suckers.
55-013.t: Banana is planted from suckers, not stem cuttings.

55-014.r: All four are propagated by stem cuttings: bougainvillea, carnation, cocoa, grapes (also sugarcane, rose, duranta); cocoa also by seeds.

55-015.r: Both true: sweet orange → grafting; jasmine → layering (part of a stem buried in soil forms roots and shoots).

55-016.r: Buds occur at both places: leaf axil (axillary bud) and tip of stem or branch (terminal bud).

55-017.r: Flower → most important part in a plant's life cycle: unites male and female gametes to produce seeds.

55-018.r: Seed germination needs water, proper temperature and oxygen; light is not required. Two types: epigeal and hypogeal.

55-020.r: Censer mechanism of seed dispersal → poppy.

55-021.r: Geitonogamy → pollen from anther to stigma of another flower on the same plant; a type of self-pollination.

55-022.r: Bat, bee and bird are all pollinating agents; bees are the most important. Pollination = transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.

55-024.r: Hybrid seed (from cross-pollinated plants) must be changed every year.

55-025.r: Seed multiplication order: nucleus → breeder → foundation → certified seed.

55-026.r: Wrong pair: plumule – root tip. Plumule = embryonic shoot; radicle = embryonic root. Correct: triple fusion – double fertilization; embryo sac – female gametophyte.

55-027.r: Dichogamy → androecium and gynoecium of a bisexual flower mature at different times; types: protandry (male first), protogyny (female first).

55-028.r: Commercial edible (bread) wheat, Triticum aestivum → ABD genome (AABBDD).

55-029.r: Maize: meiocyte 20 chromosomes, gamete 10; endosperm is triploid → 30 chromosomes.

55-030.r: Leaves receive the flowering stimulus (light, energy, CO2) and also make florigen, the flowering hormone.

56-001.r: 'Kanchan' → improved variety of Indian gooseberry (amla), rich in vitamin C; other varieties: Krishna, Banarasi.

56-002.r: Ratna mango → hybrid of Neelam (Neelum) × Alphonso; high-yielding; grown in Maharashtra and parts of Karnataka.

56-003.r: 'Kashi Lalima' → red okra (lady finger) variety from IIVR, Varanasi; rich in antioxidants, calcium and iron.

56-004.r: Co. 1148 → sugarcane variety for eastern Uttar Pradesh; medium-thick canes, good germinator, moderately drought resistant.

56-005.r: Wrong pair: linseed – Surya ('Surya' is a variety of papaya, brinjal, mango, potato, tomato). Correct: mustard – Varuna; field pea – Sapna; groundnut – Kaushal.
